paper_title: Scene-Designer: Learning Design Intelligence for Agentic 3D Scene Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating complete, coherent, and usable 3D indoor scenes from natural language requires strong \textbf{design intelligence}: the ability to design high-quality scenes and critique their quality. However, existing approaches either rely on general-purpose models lacking domain-specific design experience or learn from static scenes. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Scene-Designer}, an agentic framework that learns design intelligence through complementary design and critique experiences. We construct two datasets: \textbf{Scene-OTA-35K}, which provides Observation--Thought--Action supervision for learning scene design and efficient error correction, and \textbf{Scene-OTC-15K}, which provides Observation--Thought--Critic supervision for learning scene quality critique across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. Based on these experiences, we propose \textbf{Scene-GRPO}, a Critic-guided GRPO framework that improves design decisions and reduces unnecessary trial-and-error corrections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Scene-Designer achieves superior performance in physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while the learned Scene-Critic significantly outperforms general-purpose models in scene critique. Moreover, test-time Critic guidance further improves scene generation, showing that the Critic can provide useful guidance beyond training. Additional analysis suggests a trend of mutual enhancement between scene design and critique abilities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The clearer ones understanding becomes, the more steadfastly one acts; the more steadfastly one acts, Zhu Xi, Zhuzi yulei, vol. 14. the clearer ones understanding becomes. Automatically generating complete, coherent, and usable 3D scenes from natural-language instructions is becoming increasingly important with the rapid progress of embodied AI, automated spatial design, virtual content creation, and related applications. At its core, high-quality scene generation is not merely problem of placing objects, but problem of design. This calls for model to reason both about how scene should take shape and about the quality of the resulting scene. We refer to this capability as Design Intelligence. We define design intelligence as the ability to both design scene and critique its quality. These two capabilities correspond to two essential stages of the design process: making design decisions and evaluating their quality. Scene design concerns constructing physically valid, functionally correct, and layout-coherent scenes, while efficiently correcting errors without unnecessary trial and error when problems arise. Scene Figure 1 Overview of Design Intelligence. We define design intelligence as the ability to both design scene and critique its quality. It consists of two complementary capabilities: scene design, which constructs physically valid, functionally correct, and layout-coherent scenes while making effective corrections, and scene critique, which assesses scene quality along the same dimensions and identifies better designs. critique focuses on assessing scene quality along the same dimensions and distinguishing better designs from poorer ones. These two capabilities are closely connected, since effective design requires reliable critique to guide construction, while meaningful critique requires an understanding of what constitutes good scene design. However, even the strongest general-purpose models still exhibit clear limitations in both capabilities, as revealed by the following diagnostic studies. Challenge 1: Inefficient correction caused by unnecessary trial and error. Error correction is an essential part of scene design, but effective correction should avoid unnecessary trial and error. When the solution is straightforward, capable model should correct the error directly. To examine this behavior, we analyze the generation trajectories of GPT-5.2 with strong scene-construction scaffold. We categorize the observed construction errors into two major groups: physical errors and semantic and layout errors, each containing several fine-grained error types, as shown in Fig. 2. Our analysis of 100 generated scenes shows that GPT-5.2 can identify many design errors, yet often performs sequence of unnecessary corrective attempts before reaching an effective solution. This behavior is particularly evident for errors that could be resolved with only one or two simple operations. For example, window accessibility blockage can usually be corrected by directly moving the obstructing object, yet approximately 18% of such ases still require more than five corrective moves. Similar patterns appear across multiple error categories. These results indicate that the main limitation is not merely error recognition, but the lack of design experience needed to avoid unnecessary trial and error and perform efficient correction. Figure 2 Analysis of construction errors and correction behavior in 100 scenes generated by GPT-5.2. (a) Left: Distribution of construction errors across physical errors and semantic and layout errors. (b) Right: Distribution of corrective steps for each error category, showing that even straightforward errors often involve unnecessary trial and error before being resolved. Challenge 2: Insufficient scene critique ability. Scene critique is another essential component of design intelligence. Reliable critique requires more than recognizing obvious violations of physical validity; it must also capture whether scene is functionally correct and whether its overall layout is coherent. To examine this capability, we compare GPT-5.2 with our domain-trained model on the Scene-OTC test sets across these three dimensions. As shown in Fig. 3, GPT-5.2 achieves around 72% accuracy in pairwise scene comparison, but its performance drops to around 50% in the more challenging four-scene preference ranking. In contrast, our model consistently achieves higher accuracy across all three dimensions. Fig. 3 further illustrates representative failure case. Although Scene forms more coherent dining area by grouping functionally related furniture, GPT-5.2 prefers Scene because of its more open central space, overlooking the stronger functional organization and layout coherence of Scene A. Together, these results suggest that general-purpose models lack the scene-specific critique experience needed to reliably distinguish scene quality across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. These challenges cannot be directly addressed by existing scene data alone. Existing scene datasets, such as 3D-FRONT Fu et al. (2021) and 3D-SynthPlace Yang et al. (2026b), mainly provide static scene states with object poses, but do not capture experience from the scene design process and critique. For scene design, construction trajectories provide richer supervision, but raw trajectories often contain substantial unnecessary trial and error, reflecting the exploration process rather than effective design strategies. Extracting useful construction and correction decisions from such trajectories is therefore essential for obtaining high-quality design experience. For scene critique, the challenge is different. Many scenes can satisfy physical constraints while still differing considerably in functional correctness and layout coherence, making reliable and scalable preference supervision difficult to obtain. Effective ways to obtain such design and critique experience are therefore essential for learning design intelligence. To address these data-level challenges, we construct two complementary datasets to provide design and critique experience. For scene design, we introduce Scene-OTA-35K, containing 1K scenes and 35K Observation ThoughtAction interactions. To address trial-and-error behaviors in raw trajectories, we propose Causal Figure 3 Analysis of scene critique ability. (a) Left: Ours vs. GPT-5.2 on physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence: two-scene ranking accuracy (n = 2) and adjacent-pair ordering accuracy within four-scene rankings (n = 4). (b) Right: representative failure case of GPT-5.2 in scene critique. Trajectory Consolidation, which identifies potential ineffective operations through state and error changes, evaluates their correction effects, and preserves important correction decisions while removing ineffective corrections. For scene critique, we introduce Scene-OTC-15K, preference dataset containing 15K multi-scene comparison samples with ObservationThoughtCritic supervision. Unlike methods relying on subjective quality annotations, we generate ordered quality degradation through three types of scene perturbations with different strengths, and construct preference comparisons through three perturbation application strategies, where quality rankings can be automatically determined by perturbation strength. With these complementary experiences, we adopt two-stage training to develop design intelligence. First, joint SFT teaches the model to critique scenes in physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while constructing physically valid scenes and imitating efficient corrections, yielding Scene-Builder. We then introduce Scene-GRPO to further enable the model to design functionally correct and layout-coherent scenes while improving its correction efficiency. At each editing step, Scene-Builder explores multiple candidate actions from the same parent scene. frozen Critic provides two complementary signals by comparing candidate scenes to identify better design choices and comparing each child with its parent to assess scene improvement. These signals guide better decisions and reduce unnecessary trial and error, transforming Scene-Builder into Scene-Designer. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Scene-Designer consistently improves scene quality across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while making more effective correction decisions. For example, compared with Scene-Builder, the proportion of interaction-orientation errors requiring five or more corrective moves drops from 40% to 7%, while that of window-accessibility blockages decreases from 21% to 5%. The learned Scene-Critic also substantially outperforms general-purpose models, achieving 89% accuracy in pairwise comparison and 76% in four-scene ranking, compared with 72% and 15% for GPT-5.2, respectively. Moreover, beyond providing reward signals during training, the learned Scene-Critic can also guide scene construction at test time by selecting better editing decisions, further improving scene quality. Additional experiments reveal promising trend of mutual reinforcement between scene design and critique. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We construct two complementary datasets, Scene-OTA-35K and Scene-OTC-15K, providing effective design experience and reliable critique experience for learning design intelligence. (2) We propose Scene-GRPO, Critic-guided GRPO that leverages scene critique ability to optimize scene design decisions for high-quality scenes and reduce unnecessary trial-and-error processes. (3) Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model generates scenes with superior physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while achieving substantially stronger scene critique ability than general-purpose models.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Foundation Model-based Scene Generation. Foundation models enable language-driven 3D scene generation through semantic understanding and spatial reasoning. Early methods, such as LayoutGPT Feng et al. (2023), Figure 4 Overview of Scene-Designer. The framework learns Design Intelligence from two complementary experiences: Scene-OTA Construction extracts effective design experience from construction trajectories, while Scene-OTC Construction generates scene preference comparisons for learning critique. Together, they enable Scene-Designer to learn both scene design and critique abilities. Consolidation Statistics & Performance presents (a) the scene categories, asset counts, and asset classes in Scene-OTA-35K; (b) trajectory statistics before and after consolidation; (c) overall scene quality comparisons across methods, with scores averaged over Real., Func., Lay., and Comp. LayoutVLM Sun et al. (2025), and Holodeck Yang et al. (2024c), use LLMs or VLMs to generate scene layouts or complete 3D scenes. Recent agentic frameworks, including I-Design Çelen et al. (2024), SceneSmith Pfaff et al. (2026), and SceneWeaver Yang et al. (2026a), support iterative scene construction through tool execution and feedback. However, these approaches largely rely on general-purpose models for design decisions, which can lead to high interaction costs and inefficient error correction. Learning-based Scene Generation. Large-scale datasets, such as 3D-FRONT Fu et al. (2021) and 3DSynthPlace Yang et al. (2026b), provide scene layouts with object attributes and spatial relationships. Such scene representations have supported autoregressive Paschalidou et al. (2021), diffusion-based Tang et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2024a), and graph-based Lin and Mu (2024) generation methods. While these methods learn plausible spatial arrangements from scene collections, existing datasets mainly provide static scene states without capturing experience from the scene design process. In particular, they lack supervision on construction decisions, error corrections, and their effects on scene quality. Scene Evaluation and Critique. Existing scene evaluation methods commonly rely on geometric metrics, human preferences, or VLM-based judgments Feng et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2024c, 2026a). More recent approaches introduce structured evaluation mechanisms. SceneEval Tam et al. (2026) evaluates instruction fidelity and physical plausibility through predefined metrics, while SceneCritic Sengupta et al. (2026) employs symbolic evaluator based on statistical spatial priors to check object scales, co-occurrence, orientations, and overlaps. Although these approaches provide interpretable assessments, their predefined criteria remain limited in capturing holistic functional organization, layout coherence, and design preferences.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: As shown in Fig. 4, we develop Scene-Designer in two stages. First, joint SFT on Scene-OTA-35K and Scene-OTC-15K teaches the model to construct physically valid scenes, learn effective corrections, and critique scene quality, yielding Scene-Builder. We then introduce Scene-GRPO, which uses frozen Critic to compare candidate scenes and assess each child against its parent, guiding better design decisions and reducing unnecessary trial and error. This transforms Scene-Builder into Scene-Designer.

sections.title: 3.1 Learning Design Intelligence: From General VLM to Scene-Builder
sections.content: To provide complementary experience for scene design and critique, we construct two datasets: Scene-OTA35K and Scene-OTC-15K. Learning Scene Design with Scene-OTA. Collecting large-scale human scene-construction trajectories is costly. We therefore adopt the SceneSmith Pfaff et al. (2026) scene-construction scaffold and use GPT-5.2 to generate scenes. After manually selecting high-quality scenes, we obtain their raw construction trajectories. However, raw trajectories often contain unnecessary trial and error. To extract effective design experience, we propose Causal Trajectory Consolidation, which removes ineffective operations while preserving important construction and correction decisions. Given an original trajectory , our goal is to obtain shorter trajectory that preserves effective correction strategies and produces the same final scene state: T, S(T ) = S(T ). (1) The consolidation process consists of two stages. First, error-aware candidate identification examines each operation through changes in scene state: and remaining errors: state = D(Si1, Sf ) D(Si, Sf ) error = Vi1 Vi, (2) (3) where Si is the state after operation i, Sf is the final accepted state, D(, ) measures differences in object positions and orientations, and Vi counts remaining errors. Operations that neither improve the scene state nor reduce errors are flagged as potentially ineffective. Second, correction-effect evaluation uses GPT-5.2 to assess whether each candidate operation contributes to effective correction or necessary intermediate states, considering scene states, environment feedback, and construction context. Only ineffective operations without downstream contributions are removed. The consolidated trajectories are then replayed to verify that the final scene states remain unchanged. As shown in Fig. 4(b), consolidation reduces the average trajectory length from approximately 110 to 30 steps. For each retained action, GPT-5.2 further generates step-level reasoning traces conditioned on the current scene state, interaction history, and target action. The resulting Scene-OTA-35K contains 1K scenes and 35K ObservationThoughtAction steps, providing supervision for learning effective scene design strategies. Detailed procedures and examples are provided in Appendix D.2. Learning Scene Critique with Scene-OTC. Based on high-quality scenes from Scene-OTA, we construct Scene-OTC to provide reliable preference supervision for scene critique. We introduce three levels of scene perturbations with increasing severity: ❶Mild layout deviations preserve physical validity and functional correctness but reduce layout coherence; ❷Functional degradation disrupts functional relationships while generally maintaining physical validity; ❸Severe physical violations introduce collisions, out-of-bound placements, and other physical constraint violations. We construct ordered preference comparisons through three perturbation application strategies: ❶accumulating perturbations to progressively degrade scene quality; ❷applying perturbations of different strengths to the same object; and ❸applying the same perturbation to different objects. The first two strategies allow automatic ranking based on perturbation severity, while the third requires manual annotation, as the impact of perturbation depends on the affected objects functional role. We further use GPT-5.2 to generate reasoning traces from scene renderings and quality differences, forming ObservationThoughtCritic supervision for learning fine-grained scene quality distinctions across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. Each example contains scene renderings, reasoning trace, and complete ranking from best to worst. The resulting Scene-OTC-15K contains approximately 15K critique examples. We also construct Figure 5 Overview of Scene-GRPO. At each editing step, the policy expands multiple candidate actions from the current scene and selects the best branch to continue the trajectory. frozen Critic provides local rewards through branch ranking and parentchild comparison, while global rewards encourage efficient and complete scene design. two test sets: 94 two-scene comparisons and 55 four-scene rankings. Detailed perturbation configurations and examples are provided in Appendix D.3. Joint Supervised Fine-Tuning. Although general-purpose vision-language models possess strong visual understanding and language reasoning abilities, they lack task-specific experience for scene design and critique. We therefore jointly fine-tune the model on Scene-OTA and Scene-OTC. This SFT stage enables the model to construct physically valid scenes, imitate efficient corrections, and evaluate scene quality from the perspectives of physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, yielding Scene-Builder.

sections.title: 3.2 Critic-Guided Optimization: From Scene-Builder to Scene-Designer
sections.content: Although Scene-Builder acquires design and critique abilities through SFT, it mainly imitates existing design decisions without directly optimizing scene quality and correction efficiency. We therefore introduce SceneGRPO to improve functional correctness, layout coherence, and correction efficiency. Specifically, we initialize two copies of Scene-Builder: frozen Critic and trainable policy. Branch-Sampled Rollout. To explore alternative design decisions, Scene-GRPO samples multiple candidate actions from the same parent scene at each editing step and executes them to obtain alternative child scenes. The frozen Critic ranks the valid candidate scenes based on physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, and the highest-ranked branch is selected to continue the trajectory. Reward Design. To encourage higher-quality design decisions and reduce unnecessary trial and error, we introduce complementary local and global rewards. Two local rewards are central to Scene-GRPO. The branch-ranking reward compares sibling scenes generated from the same parent, encouraging the policy to favor better design choices. The improvement reward compares each child scene with its parent to determine whether the edit actually improves scene quality, discouraging ineffective modifications. Together, these rewards distinguish selecting better actions among alternatives from assessing whether an action leads to genuine improvement. We further introduce auxiliary rewards to support stable and efficient training. sections.title: 4 Experiment
sections.content: Training Setup. We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct as the base model and perform full-parameter fine-tuning. SFT is trained for 2 epochs with learning rate of 1 105, cosine scheduling, and 0.08 warmup ratio on 4 A800 GPUs. After SFT, we apply Scene-GRPO, where both policy and Critic are initialized from the SFT model but only the policy is updated. The policy samples 4 branches per editing step with GRPO group size of 4, maximum trajectory length of 80 steps, and learning rate of 1 106. Evaluation Metrics. Following SceneWeaver Yang et al. (2026a), we use Design me {room_type} as the unified prompt for all LLM-based methods. For each room type, each method generates 10 scenes for evaluation. Generated scenes are evaluated from two aspects: physical validity and visual-semantic quality. Physical validity is measured using objective metrics, including the number of objects (#Obj), out-of-bound objects (#OB), and object collisions (#CN). Visual-semantic quality is assessed by GPT-4 from four dimensions: realism (Real.), functionality (Func.), layout quality (Lay.), and completeness (Comp.), with each dimension scored from 0 to 10. sections.content: Figure 7 Distribution of corrective steps for each error category of Scene-Designer w/ Critic. Correction Analysis. Beyond final scene quality, we analyze correction behavior across different error categories. Compared with general-purpose models, Scene-Builder already reduces corrective steps by learning effective correction strategies from Scene-OTA. However, it still requires unnecessary corrective attempts for certain errors, motivating further optimization through Scene-GRPO. Scene-Designer substantially reduces these attempts by learning more direct and effective correction strategies. Specifically, compared with Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer reduces the proportion of cases requiring five or more corrective moves for door clearance occupation, window accessibility blockage, interaction orientation error, and scale mismatch from 15% to 13%, 21% to 5%, 40% to 7%, and 50% to 23%, respectively. These results demonstrate that Scene-GRPO helps the model avoid unnecessary trial and error and make more effective correction decisions. Furthermore, SceneDesigner w/ Critic further reduces unnecessary corrections by filtering inferior editing decisions, demonstrating the additional benefits of test-time Critic guidance. Additional cases and analyses are provided in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4.3 Design and Critique: Two Sides of the Same Coin
sections.content: Critic Reliability Evaluation. To assess Critic reliability, we evaluate pairwise scene comparison (n = 2) and four-scene ranking (n = 4) on the Scene-OTC test sets, comparing GPT-5.2, the base model, an OTC-only model, and our jointly trained Scene-OTA+OTC model. As shown in Fig. 10(a), the base model achieves 72% and 2% accuracy on = 2 and = 4, respectively, while GPT-5.2 reaches 72% and 15%. OTC fine-tuning improves performance to 86% and 51%, and joint training further raises it to 89% and 76%, demonstrating substantial gains in complex scene ranking. (a) Overall preference accuracy. (b) Detailed ranking consistency on n4. Figure 10 Evaluation of the Scene-OTC test sets. (a) compares overall preference accuracy. (b) analyzes ranking consistency with Pos-k and Top-k metrics. Fig. 10(b) further shows strong Pos-k and Top-k accuracy, indicating that our Critic can distinguish multiple quality levels rather than merely identify the best scene. To assess robustness, we shuffle the image-label order five times. As shown in Fig. 11, the Critic achieves 90.00 2.07% on = 2 and 75.64 6.88% on = 4, closely matching the original results. These findings demonstrate strong scene critique ability and consistent ranking performance, providing reliable preference supervision for Scene-GRPO. Figure 11 Image-order robustness of the learned Critic. We independently shuffle the input image-label order five times. Left: accuracy on n2 and n4 across five randomized runs. Right: Pos-k and Top-k accuracy on n4. Design as Complement of Critique To further investigate what enables reliable scene evaluation, we analyze ranking consistency on the n4 test set. Fig. 10(b) reports Pos-k and Top-k accuracy, measuring whether the k-th best scene is correctly placed and whether the top-k rankings are preserved. Scene-OTA+OTC consistently outperforms other evaluators, achieving 82% Top-1 and 76% Top-4 accuracy. These results show that scene critique is not merely visual comparison task. reliable Critic should understand both how to design and critique scene: it must recognize not only which layout is preferred, but also why certain decisions lead to better physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. This suggests that effective scene critique requires understanding the design process itself, with design knowledge serving as an essential complement to critique ability. Critique as Guidance for Design. Beyond evaluation, we naturally ask whether learning scene critique can also benefit scene design. Fig. 12 compares SFT policies trained with Scene-OTA only and Scene-OTA+OTC under identical instructions. In the dining-room example (Fig. 12(a,b)), although the Scene-OTA+OTC policy may contain minor visual imperfections, it better captures the design intent by organizing the table, chairs, buffet, and lighting into more coherent functional composition. Similarly, in the reading-focused living-room example (Fig. 9(c,d)), it establishes clearer relationships among the sofa, floor lamp, and bookshelf, forming more recognizable reading corner, while the Scene-OTAonly policy mainly satisfies object requirements with weaker functional alignment. These examples reveal an interesting trend: learning scene critique can provide complementary guidance for scene generation beyond construction trajectories alone. By understanding why certain layouts are preferred, the policy can leverage critique knowledge to make more informed design decisions and better translate high-level instructions into coherent spatial organizations and functional compositions. This suggests that design and critique are complementary aspects of design intelligence. model capable of designing well must understand the principles behind preferred layouts, and these principles can in turn guide it toward creating more coherent and functional scenes.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we introduce Scene-Designer, an agentic framework that learns design intelligence for 3D scene generation. We construct Scene-OTA and Scene-OTC to provide complementary supervision for scene design and critique, and propose Scene-GRPO for Critic-guided optimization of design decisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Scene-Designer achieves superior performance in scene generation, while suggesting that design and critique are complementary capabilities.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: Table 3 Comparison of representative scene generation methods. Existing methods lack unified framework that combines agentic tool execution, complete scene construction and scene critique ability. API Agentic Tool Complete Critique Foundation Model-based Scene Generation. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled language-driven indoor scene generation by providing strong semantic understanding and planning capabilities. As summarized in Table 3, early approaches such as LayoutGPT Feng et al. (2023), LayoutVLM Sun et al. (2025), and Holodeck Yang et al. (2024c) leverage foundation models to translate natural language instructions into structured layouts or complete 3D environments. These methods demonstrate the potential of foundation models for bridging language instructions and spatial reasoning, but typically rely on external general-purpose model APIs, resulting in substantial inference costs. LayoutGPT LayoutVLM Holodeck OptiScene SceneWeaver SceneSmith Ours Method Beyond one-shot generation, recent agentic frameworks introduce iterative construction through tool interaction. Methods including SceneCraft Hu et al. (2024), FlairGPT Littlefair et al. (2025), SceneTeller Öcal et al. (2024), I-Design Çelen et al. (2024), SceneSmith Pfaff et al. (2026), and SceneWeaver Yang et al. (2026a) enable models to progressively modify scenes through intermediate feedback and tool execution. However, these agentic approaches still rely on general-purpose models for design decisions and lack learned scene design and scene critique experience. Consequently, they may suffer from inefficient construction decisions and lengthy correction trajectories, limiting scalable scene generation. Learning-based Scene Generation and Dataset Limitations. Large-scale 3D datasets have played central role in advancing indoor scene generation. Datasets such as 3D-FRONT Fu et al. (2021) and 3D-SynthPlace Yang et al. (2026b) provide diverse indoor layouts with object categories, geometries, and spatial relationships, enabling models to learn scene distributions and generate plausible arrangements. These datasets have supported wide range of learning-based approaches, including autoregressive generation Paschalidou et al. (2021); Yang et al. (2024b), diffusion-based synthesis Tang et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2024a), and graph-based reasoning Lin and Mu (2024). Such methods improve spatial plausibility by capturing statistical regularities from large-scale scene collections. However, existing 3D datasets mainly describe static scene states rather than the design process behind them. Although they provide object categories, geometries, and spatial relationships, they do not record construction actions, error correction decisions, or quality improvements. Therefore, models trained on these datasets can learn what plausible scenes look like, but lack knowledge of how to construct and refine scenes through effective design strategies. In contrast, our work explores trajectory-based supervision that captures construction decisions, correction operations, and scene improvements. This enables models to learn not only scene distributions but also effective strategies for designing and refining scenes. Scene Evaluation and Critique. As scene generation systems become increasingly capable, evaluating generated scenes beyond geometric correctness has become essential. Existing evaluation approaches rely on geometric measurements, human preference studies, or VLM-based judgments Feng et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2024c, 2026b,a); Zhao et al. (2026). These methods typically evaluate explicit properties such as object placement, instruction compliance, and physical validity. Recent works including SceneEval Tam et al. (2026) and SceneCritic Sengupta et al. (2026) explore more structured scene evaluation beyond simple visual judgment. SceneEval combines text-scene fidelity metrics with physics-based plausibility checks, while SceneCritic introduces symbolic evaluator grounded in structured spatial ontology, verifying semantic coherence, orientation correctness, and geometric consistency through object-level and relationship-level constraints. However, existing evaluation methods remain limited in capturing holistic design qualities. Although symbolic evaluators such as SceneCritic provide reliable assessments for predefined spatial constraints, they rely on explicitly modeled relationships and handcrafted criteria, limiting their ability to assess global functional organization, layout coherence, and human-centered design preferences. In contrast, our work studies scene critique as learned design capability rather than predefined evaluation procedure. We train domain-specific VLM Critic from construction and revision experiences, enabling it to evaluate scenes across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, and further leverage critique knowledge to guide iterative scene improvement.

sections.content: D.1 Analysis of Scene Construction Errors, Correction Processes, and Editing Behaviors Category of Errors Causing Corrections. We analyze the types of errors that trigger corrections during scene construction. To understand the challenges faced by existing scene generation models, we examine failure cases and their corresponding correction operations in the original construction trajectories. We categorize the correction-triggering errors into two major families: physical errors and semantic and layout errors. Physical errors violate explicit geometric or environmental constraints, whereas semantic and layout errors occur when scene remains physically valid but fails to satisfy higher-level functional or compositional requirements. Fig. 13 summarizes the distribution of these error categories identified from 100 scenes generated by GPT-5.2. Physical errors account for 60.7% of all observed errors, while semantic and layout errors account for the remaining 39.3%. Figure 13 Category of Errors Causing Corrections. Physical errors consist of four categories. Object collision refers to interpenetration between furniture assets caused by inaccurate placement or insufficient spacing. Boundary violation occurs when objects intersect room boundaries due to improper positions, orientations, or scales. Door clearance occupation describes cases in which furniture enters door-opening or entrance area and obstructs normal access. Window accessibility blockage refers to objects placed in front of windows, restricting lighting, opening, or maintenance space. These errors primarily reflect inaccurate spatial estimation and incomplete satisfaction of geometric and environmental constraints. Semantic and layout errors consist of seven categories. Circulation and accessibility failure refers to obstructed walking paths or disconnected reachable regions caused by inappropriate furniture placement. Wall-facing orientation error occurs when wall-adjacent furniture exposes its usable side toward the wall rather than the room interior. Interaction orientation error describes interactive objects, such as chairs, facing away from their functional targets. Weak functional grouping refers to related assets that remain individually valid but fail to form coherent activity zone. Scale mismatch occurs when object dimensions deviate from realistic usage requirements. Redundant furniture describes unnecessary assets that introduce crowding or weaken the intended spatial focus. Spatial imbalance refers to an uneven distribution of furniture that disrupts the overall composition or local spacing relationships. Representative correction cases for the above error categories are presented in Figs. 14 and 15, where each case illustrates the scene before and after correction. As shown in Fig. 14(a), the object-collision case contains 4.9 cm interpenetration between desk and table, which is resolved by repositioning the table. In the boundaryviolation case, wardrobe intersects the room boundary and is moved and rotated back into the valid interior region. The door-clearance case shows cabinet entering the door-opening area; relocating it restores unobstructed access. In the windowaccessibility case, refrigerator blocks window, and relocating it recovers the usable window area. (a) Representative rework cases for physical errors. (b) Representative rework cases for selected semantic and layout errors. Figure 14 Representative rework cases for construction errors. Figs. 14(b) and 15 present representative semantic and layout corrections. In the circulation and accessibility case, the bed, nightstand, and reading-corner furniture constrain the central passage and divide the room into disconnected reachable regions. Reorganizing the bedside and reading areas and removing the redundant nightstand restore continuous circulation. In the wall-facing orientation case, dresser is placed against the wall with its functional side facing away from the room interior; rotating and realigning the dresser restore its intended usage direction. The interaction-orientation case shows dining chair facing away from the dining table, which is corrected by rotating the chair by approximately 90. In the weak functional-grouping case, an armchair and side table initially fail to form coherent reading area, whereas adjusting the chair orientation establishes clearer functional relationship. The scale-mismatch case contains an unrealistically small double vanity, which is enlarged by factor of 2.2 to obtain plausible and usable size. Figure 15 Additional representative correction cases for semantic and layout errors. In the redundant-furniture case, an additional armchair and bench weaken the dining table as the primary spatial focus; removing unnecessary furniture produces cleaner composition. Finally, the spatial-imbalance case places sideboard and display cabinet along the same side of the dining room, creating excessive visual weight. Removing the display cabinet and repositioning the sideboard yield more balanced layout. Analysis of Correction. We analyze correction behaviors from two complementary perspectives: how frequently different errors occur in construction trajectories and how many corrective moves are required to resolve them. Fig. 16 reports the trajectory-level occurrence frequency of each error category across the 100 scenes generated by GPT-5.2. We observe that construction errors occur frequently during scene generation. Physical errors appear in the majority of trajectories, with object collision, boundary violation, and door clearance occupation occurring in 91.8%, 91.8%, and 90.4% of trajectories, respectively. Window accessibility blockage also occurs in 79.5% of trajectories. Semantic and layout errors are less frequent but still appear regularly, including circulation and accessibility failure (23.3%), wall-facing orientation error (21.9%), spatial imbalance (20.5%), and interaction orientation error (19.2%). Importantly, our goal is not to require models to completely avoid all construction errors, as iterative refinement is an inherent part of scene design. Instead, effective design intelligence requires not only recognizing construction errors but also identifying efficient correction strategies. Since the same error can often be resolved through different numbers of corrective moves, correction efficiency directly affects the overall trajectory length. Figure 16 Trajectory-level occurrence probability of each error category in the original trajectories. Fig. 17 further reports the number of corrective moves required for each fine-grained error type. For each category, we measure the proportion of cases resolved with different numbers of corrective operations. The results reveal that even relatively straightforward errors can require excessive corrective operations before being resolved. We further analyze the number of corrective moves required for each error category. We focus on representative errors whose solutions often involve straightforward local modifications. For example, door clearance occupation can often be resolved by directly moving the obstructing object away from the doorway. Nevertheless, only 33% of such cases are corrected in single move, while 20% require at least five corrective moves. Similarly, window accessibility blockage usually requires only relocating the object that blocks access to the window, yet 18% of cases still involve five or more corrective moves. Orientation errors exhibit even greater inefficiency. These errors can often be corrected through directly rotating the affected object toward the room or its interaction target. However, only 12% and 7.5% of wall-facing orientation errors and interaction orientation errors are resolved in one move, respectively, while 50% and 62% require at least five moves. similar pattern appears for scale mismatch, where resizing the affected object is often sufficient, yet 42% of cases still require five or more corrective moves. More complex semantic and layout errors are even harder to resolve: 69% of circulation and accessibility failures and 47% of spatial imbalance cases involve at least five Figure 17 Distribution of corrective moves required for each error category in the original trajectories. corrective moves. These results indicate that GPT-5.2 frequently fails to identify and execute the most direct correction strategy. Instead, it performs repeated edits of object positions, orientations, or scales before reaching satisfactory solution. Since inefficient correction chains substantially extend generation trajectories, frequently occurring errors combined with ineffective corrections become major source of unnecessary interaction. Therefore, although the model can recognize many construction errors, it lacks effective correction strategies and requires excessive corrective operations even for relatively straightforward fixes. Such inefficient trajectories also increase inference cost and latency when using closed-source model APIs. Figure 18 representative asset-level editing trajectory of GPT-5.2-generated scene. (a) The editing trajectory of each major asset over the generation process, where different colors indicate different editing operations, including initial placement and subsequent reworks. (b) The final generated scene corresponding to the trajectory in (a), with major assets highlighted. Analysis of Editing Behaviors. To further understand the underlying causes of inefficient corrections, we analyze how GPT-5.2 modifies scene assets during construction. Fig. 18 visualizes the editing trajectory of individual assets in representative scene, where each node denotes an asset state and each edge represents an editing operation. We observe that the model often revisits the same assets multiple times before reaching the final configuration, indicating that many operations correspond to exploratory adjustments rather than effective correction decisions. For example, Fig. 18(b) presents representative scene generated by GPT-5.2, and Fig. 18(a) visualizes the editing trajectories of the major assets in this scene. We observe that several assets undergo repeated modifications before reaching their final states. Instead of applying targeted correction after identifying the underlying error, the model repeatedly modifies the same assets through trial and error to explore different configurations. This behavior indicates that GPT-5.2 often lacks efficient correction strategies and relies on repeated asset-level editing to gradually approach satisfactory scene. Figure 19 Statistics of asset editing frequency in GPT5.2-generated construction trajectories. The distribution shows that while many assets are placed once and never modified, considerable proportion of assets undergo repeated corrections, with some assets requiring more than five edits. We further summarize the editing frequency of assets across generated trajectories in Fig. 19. The distribution reveals highly imbalanced editing pattern: while 34% of assets are placed once and never modified, considerable proportion of assets undergo repeated corrections. Specifically, 24% of assets require five or more corrective moves, with some assets being edited up to 18 times. These repeatedly modified assets contribute disproportionately to the overall correction operations and substantially extend the trajectory length. This observation suggests that the main bottleneck is not simply the occurrence of construction errors, but the models inability to identify effective correction strategies and avoid repeated edits on the same assets. D.2 Scene-OTA Construction Overview. Scene-OTA is constructed from raw scene-construction trajectories generated by GPT-5.2 with the SceneSmith Pfaff et al. (2026) scaffold. Since raw trajectories contain many trial-and-error operations, we introduce Causal Trajectory Consolidation to remove ineffective corrections while preserving effective repair strategies. Given an original trajectory , our objective is to obtain shorter subsequence satisfying: T, S(T ) = S(T ), (22) where S(T ) denotes the final scene state produced by trajectory . Different from fixed-ratio trajectory shortening, our consolidation procedure evaluates each operation according to its contribution to scene improvement and error correction. Trajectory State Reconstruction. Before consolidation, we reconstruct intermediate scene states from tool interactions. Each asset is represented by its geometric state: sj = (xj, yj, θj, rj), (23) where (xj, yj) denotes the planar position, θj denotes the rotation angle, and rj denotes the scale factor of asset j. For each successful tool operation, we update the corresponding asset state. Specifically, move operations update the asset position and orientation, snap operations update the resulting position and orientation after applying the spatial relation, and rescale operations update the scale factor. Failed tool calls are ignored since they do not modify the actual scene state. Error-aware Candidate Identification. We first identify potentially ineffective operations using two complementary signals: geometric progress toward the final state and reduction of construction errors. Given an operation ai, we compare the scene states before and after the operation with the final accepted scene state Sf . Here, Si denotes the complete scene state after operation i, which consists of all asset states. Specifically, we define the state progress as: state = D(Si1, Sf ) D(Si, Sf ), (24) where Si1 and Si denote the scene states before and after operation i, respectively. D(, ) measures the difference between two scene states. For each asset state, we first define the asset-level distance as: where dp is the Euclidean distance between asset positions: Da(si, sf ) = λpdp(si, sf ) + λθdθ(si, sf ), dp(si, sf ) = (xi xf )2 + (yi yf )2, and dθ measures the angular difference: dθ(si, sf ) = wrap(θi θf ). (25) (26) (27) The scene-level distance is computed by aggregating the distances of all assets: D(Si, Sf ) = Da(si,j, sf,j), (28) where si,j and sf,j denote the states of asset before and after consolidation. positive state value indicates that it deviates from the final state. indicates that the operation moves the scene closer to its final configuration, while negative In addition to geometric progress, we evaluate whether an operation reduces existing construction errors: error = Vi1 Vi, (29) where Vi denotes the number of remaining construction errors after operation i. The error set includes both physical errors and semantic and layout errors. Physical errors are obtained from environment feedback, which provides explicitly detectable constraint violations, including object collisions, boundary violations, door clearance occupation, and window accessibility blockage. Semantic and layout errors are identified through scene evaluation feedback. An operation that neither improves the final state distance nor reduces existing construction errors is regarded as suspicious trial-and-error operation and becomes candidate for further causal evaluation. Correction-Effect Evaluation. The above rule-based criteria are designed to identify potentially ineffective operations with high recall, but they cannot determine whether an operation is truly unnecessary. Some operations may temporarily increase the distance to the final state while establishing intermediate configurations required by subsequent corrections. Therefore, we further employ GPT-5.2 as causal verifier to evaluate the contribution of each candidate operation. For each candidate operation, GPT-5.2 receives the following information: (1) the original room instruction; (2) the scene states before and after the candidate operation; (3) the final accepted scene state; (4) the operation description and tool parameters; (5) surrounding operations before and after the candidate operation; (6) available environment feedback or semantic scene-evaluation feedback; and (7) rule-based screening signals, including final-state progress state , segment-level error reduction error , operation reversal, and immediate overwrite. We additionally provide the definitions of construction-error categories, enabling the verifier to associate each operation with the corresponding error being corrected. Given these inputs, the verifier evaluates whether each operation makes meaningful contribution to the correction process. Specifically, each candidate operation is assigned one of three labels: yi redundant_trial, useful_correction, uncertain. (30) An operation is classified as redundant_trial when it provides no meaningful contribution to resolving the identified error and can be removed without affecting the final correction result. Typical cases include true no-operations, ineffective adjustments that are later reversed, intermediate placements immediately overwritten by subsequent absolute placements, or operations unrelated to the reported construction error. However, reversal or overwrite alone is insufficient for removal: an operation is retained if it reduces an existing error or provides useful intermediate correction experience. An operation is classified as useful_correction when it resolves or substantially reduces an existing error, establishes an intermediate state required by later operations, or forms necessary component of coordinated multi-object correction. In particular, an operation remains useful even when later operation further refines its result. Operations whose contribution cannot be reliably determined, for example when the effect of multiple operations cannot be isolated, are labeled as uncertain and conservatively retained. The verifier returns structured response containing the predicted label, confidence score, and brief causal explanation for each candidate operation. It also identifies operations recommended for retention or removal. An operation is considered removable only when it is classified as redundant_trial with confidence higher than τ . The verifier output is treated as deletion proposal rather than final decision; protected operations and operations with downstream dependencies are retained regardless of the predicted label. Causal Trajectory Consolidation. After causal evaluation, we consolidate the original trajectory by removing only operations identified as unnecessary while preserving causally important correction decisions. Specifically, an operation ai is removed only when it satisfies three conditions: (1) it is identified as suspicious candidate in the error-aware candidate identification stage; (2) it is classified as redundant_trial by the causal verifier; and (3) its confidence score is higher than the threshold τ . Formally, the removal set is defined as: = {ai Ci = 1, yi = redundant_trial, pi τ } , (31) where Ci indicates whether operation ai is selected as suspicious candidate by the rule-based screening stage, yi denotes the verifier prediction, and pi denotes the verifier confidence. In our implementation, we set τ = 0.8. To avoid removing necessary construction decisions, we apply conservative constraints during consolidation. Operations that modify asset existence, including object addition and removal, are always retained. We also preserve operations that reduce construction errors, establish intermediate states required by subsequent operations, or contribute to coordinated multi-object corrections. When multiple operations modify the same asset, the final effective correction is retained. After consolidation, we manually review the trajectories to verify their quality and remove remaining inconsistent cases. The consolidated trajectory is obtained by removing the selected operations while preserving the temporal order of the remaining operations: = Remove(T, R). (32) For each removed operation, its corresponding tool call and environment feedback are removed together, while the remaining operations preserve the original temporal order. The consolidated trajectory is finally verified through replay to ensure that it produces the same final scene state as the original trajectory. Consolidation Statistics. To analyze the effect of Causal Trajectory Consolidation, we compare the composition of raw and consolidated trajectories in Fig. 20. Beyond removing ineffective trial-and-error corrections, consolidation eliminates several types of low-value operations, including read-only calls that do not modify the scene state and failed tool calls that produce no effective changes. For error-recovery trajectories, we preserve the operation that introduces the error and the final effective correction while removing unnecessary intermediate repair attempts. Efficient correction trajectories remain unchanged. As shown in Fig. 20, Causal Trajectory Consolidation reduces the average number of tool calls per trajectory by 57%. Specifically, read-only calls, which account for 41.9% of raw trajectory steps, and repeated retries caused by trialand-error behaviors are removed, while essential placement operations and effective error-correction operations are preserved. These results demonstrate that consolidation Figure 20 Effect of Causal Trajectory Consolidation on trajectory composition. The consolidation removes read-only calls, failed calls, and repeated retries while preserving essential placement and effective correction operations, reducing the average number of tool calls per trajectory by 57%. does not simply shorten trajectories, but selectively removes ineffective behaviors while retaining the causal decisions required for successful scene construction. To illustrate the design experience captured by Scene-OTA, Fig. 21 presents representative consolidated construction trajectory. The trajectory records not only the initial scene planning decisions but also intermediate feedback and effective correction decisions, showing how the model progressively improves the scene through iterative design. D.3 Scene-OTC Construction Overview. Scene-OTC provides preference supervision for scene critique learning by applying controlled perturbations to high-quality scenes in Scene-OTA. Instead of binary labels, it creates degraded variants with different design qualities, enabling the Critic to learn fine-grained preferences and understand why one scene is preferred over another. We organize perturbations into three increasing levels of severity: ❶mild layout deviations, which preserve physical validity and functionality but reduce visual harmony or spatial balance; ❷functional degradation, which disrupts object relations, interaction orientations, or functional grouping while generally maintaining physical validity; and ❸severe physical violations, which introduce explicit geometric failures such as collisions and out-of-bound placement. The perturbation categories and corresponding operations are summarized in Tab. 4, and detailed definitions are provided in Tab. 5. Preference Annotation and Reasoning Generation. For each perturbation strategy, we construct preference examples containing scene renderings. The preference order of accumulating perturbations and differentstrength perturbations is automatically determined according to the perturbation severity. For the same perturbation applied to different objects, the preference order is manually annotated because the impact depends on the functional role of each object in the scene. Given the scene renderings and the corresponding instruction, GPT-5.2 is further used to generate reasoning traces that explain the quality differences and produce complete preference rankings from best to worst. Each example follows the ObservationThoughtCritic format, providing supervision for the model to identify and explain fine-grained differences in physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence.
