Move an object into corner, producing less reasonable spatial distribution. Apply an unnatural rotation offset while maintaining physical validity. Perturbation Strategies. To construct preference examples with different levels of difficulty, we design three perturbation strategies that capture complementary aspects of scene quality. First, accumulating perturbations create ordered degradation chains by progressively adding new perturbations to an initially high-quality scene. Each subsequent scene inherits previous defects and introduces additional degradation, resulting in naturally ordered preferences from high to low quality. Second, different-strength perturbations apply the same modification to the same object with increasing severity levels. These examples teach the Critic to distinguish subtle quality differences, where mild perturbations may only weaken spatial coherence while stronger perturbations significantly damage functional relationships. Third, same perturbation on different objects applies identical modifications to objects with different functional roles. Since the impact of perturbation depends on the affected object, these examples require the Critic to consider object importance and scene context rather than relying only on the perturbation type. Representative examples of the three perturbation strategies are shown in Fig. 22. In Fig. 22(a), accumulating perturbations construct an ordered degradation chain from high-quality scene. Starting from the original layout, each subsequent scene introduces one additional perturbation while preserving previous defects. This Figure 21 representative Scene-OTA trajectory. The trajectory records the complete scene construction process creates naturally ranked scene variants, allowing the Critic to understand how accumulated errors progressively reduce overall scene quality. In Fig. 22(b), different-strength perturbations apply the same modification to the same object with different severity levels. For example, gradually moving an object away from its functional partner produces increasingly degraded layouts: mild displacement may only weaken object relationships, whereas stronger displacement can disrupt functional coherence. These examples encourage the Critic to capture fine-grained quality differences rather than treating perturbations as binary failures. In Fig. 22(c), same perturbation on different objects applies the same modification to objects with different functional importance. Although identical operations may be applied, their impact on scene quality varies depending on the objects role. For example, removing primary functional object causes more severe degradation than removing secondary decorative object. These examples require the Critic to reason about object roles and scene context when producing preferences. (b) Different-strength perturbations (c) Same perturbation on different objects (a) Accumulating perturbations Figure 22 Representative perturbation strategies in Scene-OTC. (a) Accumulating perturbations progressively degrade scene quality by introducing additional defects. (b) Different-strength perturbations apply the same modification with varying severity. (c) The same perturbation applied to different objects reveals the influence of object functional importance. Dataset Statistics. Following the above construction process, we obtain Scene-OTC-15K, containing approximately 15K scene critique examples. Each example contains multiple scene renderings, complete preference ranking, and reasoning trace generated by GPT-5.2. In addition, we construct two-scene comparison test set with 94 examples and four-scene ranking test set with 55 examples for evaluating scene critique ability. Critique Capabilities Covered by Scene-OTC. The perturbation hierarchy in Scene-OTC is designed to enhance three complementary scene critique abilities. Physical validity focuses on recognizing explicit geometric and environmental violations, including collisions, boundary violations, and accessibility failures. Functional correctness requires understanding object roles, interaction orientations, and functional relationships, where scene can remain physically valid but fail to support intended usage. Layout coherence captures higherlevel scene organization, including spatial balance, object grouping, and global composition quality, where degradation may be subtle and difficult to identify from local object changes. By covering these three dimensions, Scene-OTC enables the Critic to evaluate scenes beyond simple validity checking and develop more comprehensive understanding of scene quality.

sections.title: E Case Study
sections.content: This section provides additional qualitative analyses to complement the quantitative results in the main paper. We first compare Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer, and Scene-Designer with Critic across representative room types, then examine how the learned Critic guides branch selection during inference, and finally present comparisons between Scene-Designer and existing methods. Together, these cases illustrate the effects of SFT, Scene-GRPO, and test-time Critic guidance on scene quality, construction behavior, and intermediate design decisions. E.1 Examples of Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer, and Scene-Designer with Critic We provide additional qualitative comparisons to complement the quantitative results in the main paper. Each case compares Scene-Builder, SceneDesigner, and Scene-Designer with Critic under the same instruction, together with their corresponding construction trajectories. These examples illustrate how SFT provides basic scene construction ability, while RL improves functional organization and Critic guidance further enables more deliberate intermediate decision making. As shown in Fig. 23(a-c), Scene-Builder can generate physically valid scenes but often lacks coherent functional organization, resulting in less structured layouts under the same instruction. While Scene-Builder can generate physically valid scenes, it often lacks consideration of functional correctness and layout coherence. In contrast, Scene-Designer and Scene-Designer w/ Critic produce scenes that better satisfy all three design requirements, including physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, indicating that SceneGRPO enables the model to better reason about design requirements before execution. We further analyze the editing trajectories of major assets in Fig. 23(df). Scene-Builder frequently relies on trial-and-error corrections, where objects are repeatedly adjusted after suboptimal initial decisions. Figure 23 Trajectory analysis under the instruction: Design serene master bedroom centered on queen bed with matching nightstands and reading lamps, with dresser placed against the opposite wall to create calm and relaxing atmosphere. (a,d,g), (b,e,h), and (c,f,i) correspond to Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer, and Scene-Designer w/ Critic, respectively. (ac) Generated scenes under the same instruction. (df) Editing trajectories of major assets during construction. (gi) Distributions of corrective edits per object over 100 generated scenes. By learning sequential construction experience and optimizing editing choices through Critic-guided GRPO, Scene-Designer performs more deliberate modifications and avoids unnecessary revisions. With additional test-time Critic guidance, Scene-Designer w/ Critic further improves intermediate decision selection by filtering inferior editing alternatives before execution. Fig. 23(g-i) summarizes the distribution of object-level corrective edits over 100 generated scenes. Compared with Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer increases the proportion of objects placed once and never modified from 46% to 56%, while reducing heavily corrected objects (more than five corrections) from 15% to 10%. Scene-Designer w/ Critic further improves these trends, achieving 58% untouched objects and reducing heavily corrected cases to only 5%. These results show that Critic-guided optimization does not simply shorten trajectories; instead, it enables the model to make more reliable design decisions before execution, leading to more efficient and coherent scene construction. Additionally, we provide several more representative cases as follows. Fig. 24 presents family kitchen example requiring cabinet storage, an efficient cooking workflow among the refrigerator, range, and preparation area, as well as dining zone for everyday meals. Scene-Builder produces physically valid kitchen and satisfies most object requirements, but the overall arrangement is relatively object-centric: the cooking components and dining furniture are less clearly organized into functional zones, and several assets require repeated adjustments during construction. After RL optimization, Scene-Designer generates more structured layout, where the kitchen appliances, storage units, and dining table form clearer functional groups. Scene-Designer with Critic further improves the result by selecting better intermediate branches during construction, preserving circulation space and producing more coherent relationship between cooking and dining areas. The trajectory comparison shows that Critic guidance helps avoid unnecessary corrections and leads to more purposeful refinement. Figure 24 The evaluated instruction is: Create family kitchen built for cooking togetherplenty of cabinet storage, range and fridge grouped for an efficient work triangle, and dining table with chairs for everyday meals. Qualitative comparison across SFT, RL, and test-time Critic guidance. (a,d), (b,e), and (c,f) correspond to Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer, and Scene-Designer with Critic, respectively. Fig. 25 shows family dining-room example requiring wooden table with six chairs, buffet for storage, and soft overhead lighting. SceneBuilder generates reasonable dining environment but exhibits weaker functional grouping, with furniture elements lacking clear relationship centered around the dining activity. SceneDesigner improves the spatial organization by placing the table, chairs, buffet, and lighting elements into more coherent dining composition, better matching the intended family-meal scenario. With test-time Critic guidance, SceneDesigner further refines intermediate choices by favoring layouts with stronger functional connections and balanced spatial distribution. As reflected in the construction trajectories, Criticguided generation requires fewer unnecessary modifications while maintaining more consistent design process. Figure 25 The evaluated instruction is: Create warm family dining room with sturdy wooden table and six chairs, buffet for dishes and linens, and soft overhead lighting for everyday dinners. Qualitative comparison across SFT, RL, and testtime Critic guidance. (a,d), (b,e), and (c,f) correspond to Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer, and Scene-Designer with Critic, respectively. Figure 26 The evaluated instruction is: Create spa-like bathroom Create spa-like bathroom with separate shower, sleek vanity with large mirror, and calm, minimal finishes. Qualitative comparison across SFT, RL, and test-time Critic guidance. (a,d), (b,e), and (c,f) correspond to Scene-Builder, Scene-Designer, and Scene-Designer with Critic, respectively. Fig. 26 presents spa-like bathroom example involving separate shower, vanity with large mirror, and calm minimal finishes. Scene-Builder can construct the required bathroom elements, but the generated layout relies more on local placement decisions and may contain weaker relationships among major functional components. Scene-Designer improves the arrangement by learning higher-level spatial organization, creating clearer separation between the shower area, vanity zone, and remaining functional space. Scene-Designer with Critic further enhances the final layout by filtering less suitable construction alternatives, resulting in more balanced and coherent bathroom design. This case demonstrates that Critic guidance is beneficial not only for avoiding physical errors but also for improving subtle functional and aesthetic decisions during scene creation. E.2 Test-Time Critic Guidance Examples To better understand how the learned Critic guides scene generation during inference, we provide representative construction example in Fig. 27. Given the instruction of creating cozy reading-focused living room, the Scene-Designer policy performs iterative construction through multiple editing steps. At each step, instead of directly executing single action, the policy samples multiple candidate branches with different object additions, removals, or modifications. The learned Critic then evaluates these intermediate layouts based on physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, and selects the branch with the highest design quality for further construction. In the first stage, the policy generates four candidate layouts after the initial construction. The Critic ranks Scene as the preferred choice because it better satisfies the design requirements: the sofa serves as the central anchor, the coffee table remains within reach of the seating area, the media console maintains clear viewing relationship, and the bookshelf is positioned without obstructing circulation. In contrast, other candidates exhibit weaker functional correctness and layout coherence. For example, Scene places the media console near the window, weakening the relationship between the viewing area and seating zone, while Scene creates mismatched focal arrangement between the sofa and media console. Scene further suffers from disconnected seating arrangement, where the sofa, armchair, and coffee table fail to form coherent functional group. By identifying these differences, the Critic guides the policy toward better intermediate scene state. As construction continues, the Critic repeatedly filters out inferior editing decisions and encourages modifications that improve the overall scene quality. In later steps, candidate branches involve operations such Figure 27 Test-time Critic guidance during scene construction. The Scene-Designer samples multiple candidate branches at each step, and the Scene-Critic ranks intermediate layouts based on physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. The selected branches progressively refine the scene toward the final design. as removing unnecessary furniture, adding missing assets, or adjusting object configurations. The Critic does not simply favor scenes with more objects; instead, it evaluates whether each modification improves functional correctness and layout coherence while maintaining physical validity. For example, when selecting among branches with different furniture removals, the Critic prefers layouts that preserve essential functional elements, maintain balanced seating relationships, and avoid circulation conflicts. Similarly, when evaluating object additions, it favors branches where newly introduced furniture strengthens existing functional groups rather than creating isolated or redundant elements. After several rounds of Critic-guided selection, the final scene achieves more coherent reading-oriented living environment. The sofa, coffee table, accent chair, floor lamp, and bookshelf form meaningful spatial relationships, creating both primary conversation area and secondary reading corner. Compared with unguided trial-and-error exploration, this process avoids unnecessary corrections by selecting promising intermediate states before committing to further construction. This example highlights that the learned Critic is not merely reward estimator used during GRPO optimization. Instead, it captures transferable scene design preferences regarding physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, allowing it to serve as an inference-time decision assistant. By evaluating alternative construction branches and guiding the policy toward better intermediate layouts, the Critic enables more deliberate and efficient scene generation. In addition, Fig. 28 presents representative example of using GPT-5.2 as test-time critic for guiding scene construction. Although GPT-5.2 provides detailed rationales for each branch selection, its judgments are often inconsistent with the actual scene quality. In the first selection step, GPT-5.2 prefers Scene by emphasizing balanced seating arrangement and clear circulation. However, this judgment overlooks that Scene provides weaker functional organization: the sofa, chair, and coffee table do not form as coherent reading and conversation area as Scene A. Similarly, in later decisions, GPT-5.2 tends to focus on isolated visual cues, such as open space or apparent object alignment, while missing more important design factors including object relationships and functional usability. In the third branch selection, GPT-5.2 selects Scene as the best candidate while overlooking clear physical validity issue: the table and floor lamp are placed in collision. In contrast, Scene avoids this collision and maintains more reasonable spatial arrangement. This indicates that GPT-5.2 may recognize general layout patterns but fails to consistently verify explicit geometric constraints when multiple factors compete. In the final branch selection, GPT-5.2 again prefers Scene B, although Scene provides better overall composition. Scene places furniture too densely in the corner and reverses the functional orientation of the cabinet, weakening both layout coherence and functional correctness. These examples show that general-purpose models may produce plausible explanations but still lack reliable scene-specific criteria for evaluating physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. These observations reveal that general-purpose closed-source models lack stable evaluation criteria across the three key dimensions of scene quality. Although GPT-5.2 can generate reasonable explanations based on visual observations, its preferences may be inconsistent with actual design requirements: it can overlook explicit physical violations, focus on local object arrangements rather than functional relationships, or favor visually open layouts while ignoring global spatial organization. Therefore, directly using such models as test-time critics can provide unreliable guidance, causing the policy to select inferior intermediate states and limiting the effectiveness of inference-time scene optimization. This motivates the need for domain-specific Critic trained with structured scene-quality supervision to provide more consistent guidance during scene construction. E.3 Examples of Scene-Designer and Other Methods Figure 29 presents representative comparisons between our Scene-Designer and existing scene generation methods across diverse indoor environments, including bathrooms, dining rooms, kitchens, living rooms, and offices. Existing methods often struggle to generate complete and functionally coherent scenes. For example, LayoutGPT and LayoutVLM frequently produce incomplete environments or only arrange subset of major furniture while missing important structural elements such as walls, windows, mirrors, wall-mounted objects, and lighting fixtures. In several cases, generated layouts also contain obvious physical issues, including object Figure 28 representative failure case of GPT-5.2 as test-time Critic during scene construction. GPT-5.2 often provides plausible rationales but fails to consistently evaluate physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence when selecting among candidate branches. collisions, unreasonable object density, and insufficient circulation space. For instance, in the dining room and living room cases, some methods place furniture without considering functional grouping, resulting in isolated objects and poorly organized activity areas. Similarly, in kitchen and office scenarios, objects are often arranged without considering practical usage relationships, leading to layouts that are physically plausible but functionally ineffective. Compared with these approaches, Scene-Builder consistently generates complete scenes with valid room structures and satisfies basic physical constraints. However, as shown in the examples, its layouts may still lack higher-level design considerations, such as optimal functional organization and spatial balance. After applying Scene-GRPO, Scene-Designer further improves scene quality by learning effective construction and correction strategies from design trajectories. It produces more coherent arrangements, such as grouping functionally related objects, maintaining appropriate interaction spaces, and balancing furniture distribution within the room. Moreover, incorporating the learned Critic during inference further enhances the generated Figure 29 Qualitative comparison between Scene-Designer and existing scene generation methods. Existing methods often generate incomplete scenes or suffer from physical violations, poor functional organization, and incoherent layouts. Scene-Builder produces physically valid scenes, while Scene-Designer further improves functional correctness and layout coherence through learned design strategies. Adding the Critic during inference provides additional guidance and further enhances overall scene quality. scenes by providing additional quality guidance, leading to improvements across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence.

sections.title: F Prompts
sections.content: F.1 System Prompts We adopt the scene-construction scaffold introduced by SceneSmith Pfaff et al. (2026). Since the scaffold provides large number of tools for different construction operations, following SceneSmith, we decompose the generation process into multiple stages: ❶ defining the overall room structure, including room dimensions, door and window placement, and material settings; ❷ placing large floor-standing assets; ❸ adding wall-mounted assets; and ❹ adding ceiling-mounted assets. During inference, each stage is associated with different system prompt that specifies its current construction objective and available operations. When the model produces only reasoning trace without an executable tool call, we interpret this as the completion of the current stage. In the following step, the system prompt is replaced with the predefined prompt for the next stage. Although the construction process is divided into multiple stages, we treat all stages as unified generation process and record them as single ObservationThoughtAction trajectory. We next introduce the system prompt used at each stage. The system prompts follow unified template across different construction stages, where only stage-specific fields are replaced according to the current construction objective. Specifically, stage_role defines the role of the model in the current stage, stage_task and stage_prompt specify the construction objective, and stage_scope restricts the assets that can be created or modified. The workflow field provides the recommended construction procedure, while stage_specific_guidelines and stage_specific_annotations incorporate stage-dependent constraints and rendering interpretations. The available tools are also dynamically specified according to each stage. Therefore, although different stages use different system prompts, they share the same overall structure and only differ in stage-specific configurations. Figure 30 System prompt template. F.2 Memory Snapshot In our framework, Mt denotes structured memory snapshot provided to the policy at each reasoning step. Instead of storing the complete interaction trajectory, Mt summarizes the essential information required for continued scene construction. As shown in Fig. 31, the memory snapshot contains three components: the current stage state, physical validation status, and recent tool interactions. The stage_state records the scene information Its relevant to the current construction stage. content changes according to the stage objective: the floor-plan stage describes the room structure, doors, windows, and materials; the furniture stage describes placed assets and their configurations; and the wall and ceiling stages record the corresponding mounted objects and placement states. The physics_status provides the latest environment validation results, including detected physical violations that require correction. The final component maintains the most recent tool interactions, including executed tool calls and their returned results, allowing the model to track recent decisions without repeatedly revisiting the full trajectory history. Figure 31 Unified memory snapshot template used by the policy model across different construction stages. At each step, the rendered memory snapshot is provided together with the system prompt, task instruction, and current scene observation. After successful tool execution, the memory is updated according to the returned tool result: Mt+1 = pdate(Mt, at, ft), (33) where at denotes the executed tool call and ft denotes the corresponding tool feedback. F.3 Correction-Effect Evaluation Prompt For correction-effect evaluation, we provide GPT-5.2 with structured JSON input describing each candidate correction segment. The placeholder {SEGMENT_JSON} is dynamically replaced by the candidate segment data extracted from the original trajectory. It contains segment-level information, operation-level states, Figure 32 Prompt template for correction-effect evaluation. The verifier receives structured trajectory evidence and outputs operation-level causal judgments. geometric progress signals, feedback changes, and object lifecycle context. Each operation record includes the executed tool call and arguments, object identity, scene states before and after the operation, final accepted state, final-state progress, and screening signals. The feedback fields record error changes from environment validation and semantic revision feedback, while the object lifecycle context provides nearby operations to identify potential dependencies. Given this structured input, GPT-5.2 predicts an operation-level label: yi redundant_trial, useful_correction, uncertain. (34) The output is formatted as strict JSON object containing the segment-level judgment, operation-level labels, confidence scores, and brief causal explanations. The complete prompt template is shown in Fig. 32.

sections.content: Due to space limitations in the main paper, we present several additional experiments and analyses in this section to further evaluate our method from complementary perspectives. These metrics are computed directly from room geometry and final asset placements without using GPT or rendered images, providing more objective assessment of scene accessibility and spatial organization. Reachability Ratio. This metric evaluates whether the free space in scene is well connected. For an agent with width w, we shrink the room boundary by w/2 and expand each furniture footprint by w/2, so that the agent is treated as having non-zero body width rather than as point. The results demonstrate that the proposed training strategy consistently improves the geometric quality of generated scenes. Scene-Designer already achieves strong accessibility performance compared with Scene-Builder, with higher RR@0.3, RR@0.5, and FR@0.3, indicating that Scene-GRPO enables the model to better organize objects and preserve connected free space during construction. After introducing the Critic, Scene-Designer w/ Critic further improves the overall spatial organization, achieving the highest RR across different agent widths, the best mRR (0.98), complete full reachability (FR@0.3=1.0), and the highest navigable area ratio. These results suggest that Critic-guided optimization helps the model avoid locally plausible but spatially inefficient arrangements and select layouts with better global accessibility. The door and window accessibility metrics further show that all proposed models maintain strong environmental constraints. All methods achieve perfect DAR, while Scene-Designer w/ Critic additionally achieves the highest WAR, indicating that Critic guidance helps preserve accessibility around important environmental structures such as windows. Overall, these geometry-based metrics provide complementary evidence that Scene-Designer and Scene-Designer w/ Critic generate scenes with improved spatial organization and accessibility, beyond the GPT-based quality evaluations and basic collision statistics reported in the main experiments.
